label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
**Cup Day 2026: The Day the Coolroom Quit On Us (And You Missed The Whole Thing)**

*Posted 10 Nov 2026 — for Jonno, who has asked four times now.*

---

Jonno.

You've messaged me about this every three days since the story went up, which is very on brand for a man who now lives somewhere with an actual Waitrose. Fine. Here it is. The whole stupid thing, written down properly, so you can read it in your little rented flat in London with your little flat white and send me a thumbs up emoji like you're on a bus.

I'll start at the top.

**6.40am, Tuesday 3 November. Cup Day.**

The coolroom compressor died overnight. Not "we had a temp issue" died — died, properly, the way a fridge gives up when it's been asked to do too much for six years and one hot Melbourne spring.

You know the walk-in? The big one, the one with the door that sticks and the gasket you keep meaning to replace? It was sitting there at quarter to seven in the morning reading 11 degrees. Not 11 Celsius. Eleven. I know. I know what you're about to type, Jonno, and the answer is yes, in the walk-in, in November. The compressor had been dead for hours and the room had been slowly becoming a room full of warm milk.

I opened the door and it was like walking into a car park. The duck legs were doing something I don't want to describe to you because you're in London now and you don't need that in your head before breakfast.

**The brief:** Cup Day lunch. 140 covers booked. Set menu. Three courses. A number we wrote down ourselves in July when we were feeling brave.

**The plan:** Wally from Coldline was our man. Wally is a legend. Wally is also a man who works on a Tuesday, and this particular Tuesday his technician was in Gippsland pulling a part out of a fish freezer in the back of a pub. The part was coming from Sydney. It would arrive Wednesday.

Wednesday is the day after Cup Day.

So we had roughly nine hours to run a 140-cover three-course lunch with no coolroom.

**The workaround.**

Everything went into three places: the two undercounters, the bar fridge, and half of Marta's walk-in next door, which Marta very generously lent us at about 6.50am while I was standing in the street with my hair on fire.

Marta runs the little cafe next door. Eight tables, gorgeous, all plants and ceramics and a espresso machine worth more than my car. And she looked at me — actual mess, apron on inside out — and said "take what you need."

I love Marta. I also now owe Marta approximately three weeks of staff meals in croissant credit, which is a payment plan I did not agree to and cannot afford. Every time I see her I have to do a mental calculation like a debt collector. "Hey Marta, how's the— how many croissants would cover... no, more than that... no, less croissants but good ones..."

**The maths of a bar fridge.**

Here's what I learned on Cup Day: a bar fridge is not a walk-in. A bar fridge is where you keep the stuff that has to survive until Friday, and on Cup Day the bar fridge became the entire dairy operation of a 140-cover restaurant. Every yoghurt, every cream, every block of butter in the building ended up in there, stacked in towers like a game of Jenga written by someone who hates you.

We lost about $1,800 of stock. Mostly dairy, which was the bit we couldn't swap, and the duck legs, which is a number I'm still pretending isn't real. A duck leg is about fifteen bucks and we had a lot of them and they are all gone. Gone. Into warm air. Into the universe.

**No Raff.** Our head chef was away that day, which meant the pass was mine, which meant when the compressor was dead I had nobody to hide behind. Not that I'd hide. But you understand. When you've got a head chef in the building they handle the panic and you just do your section. Me and Benny ended up doing everything, including the things that aren't my section, including the things nobody's section is.

**The shin.**

Thirty kilos of beef shin. Down the laneway. On a milk crate trolley. In the rain.

There is a milk crate trolley in the kitchen that has one bad wheel, and that wheel has been bad for two years, and on Cup Day in the rain it finally made its choice. It left. Somewhere in the middle of the laneway the wheel came off and the trolley did a thing I can only describe as a slow, dignified betrayal. Benny grabbed the crate. I grabbed the other end. We carried thirty kilos of shin down a wet laneway with a milk crate between us like we were loading a boat.

We got it inside. The floor was wet. There was beef juice on the wet floor. I want to be very clear that we did not slip. We did not slip, Jonno. But there was a moment. There was a definite moment where the floor won.

**Kev and the esky.**

Our dishwasher Kev is the most underestimated man in Australian hospitality and he deserves a medal, a statue, a plaque. He took the old esky — the big blue one that lives under the bench and hasn't been used since 2019 — and filled it with ice from the servo down the road.

Fourteen bags.

He made about nine trips. And the guy at the servo, who knows Kev, watched this happen and walked over and said, "You having a party?"

Fourteen bags of ice. Into an esky. In a car park. At 8am.

"No," Kev said. "We just lost our fridge."

And the servo guy said, "Good luck with that," which is the single most Australian sentence ever spoken, and then charged us full price for twenty-six kilos of ice.

**12.15pm: the panna cotta gets 86'd.**

The panna cotta was set in ramekins and it needed the walk-in to set properly overnight. Obviously it was in the walk-in. Obviously.

So at a quarter past twelve, on the day, with lunch already running, I made a decision. We 86'd the panna cotta.

What replaced it: affogato with whatever.

I want to give a shout out to whoever decided that on a day like this, when everything was going wrong, the answer isn't to apologise — the answer is to just do something hot, cold and boozy with coffee and sugar and whatever cream survived. We had about a third of a litre of cream left. We had a lot of coffee. We had Marsala in the bottle we use for the chicken dish, because of course we did, and the dishwashing situation was such that nobody was checking.

And it worked. Genuinely. People ate the affogato and then asked what it was, and when we told them, they said, "oh, that's way better than a panna cotta," which is a lie, it is not better than a panna cotta, but I loved them for it, and honestly it might have been better than the panna cotta.

**Table 9.**

A lady at table nine, mid-main, looked out the window at the laneway where Benny and I had just been doing the shin carry with our trolley minus one wheel.

She said, "Is the beef free range from the laneway?"

I said, "It is now, actually. The wheel fell off."

She said, "That's beautiful."

It was not beautiful. It was a wet laneway and a broken trolley. But she was happy. Table nine was happy. Table nine ate everything and left a decent tip and I would do it all again.

**The bit Phil said.**

At about nine in the morning, in the middle of all this, the owner came in. Phil. Lovely bloke. Absolute legend in the way that means "he will not open his wallet" — full respect, we all work together, I mean it.

He looked at the walk-in reading 11 degrees. He looked at me. He said:

"Just make it work mate."

Which is a great sentence. Which is a beautiful sentence. Which is not a plan. "Just make it work mate" is what you say to a bloke at 7am on Cup Day when you're already doing the work of four people and you've lost a thousand eight hundred bucks of stock before doors open. It is not a plan. It is a vibe. It's a hand on the shoulder from a man who is not carrying a milk crate.

So I made it work. We made it work. But I want it on the record that "just make it work mate" is not a plan, and if anyone from the media is reading this, that's my submission.

**The service.**

And here's the thing, Jonno, the thing I actually wanted to tell you.

We did the best service of the year that night. Best of the whole year.

140 covers. Three courses, set menu, one dessert that didn't exist when the menu was printed. The dining room didn't know anything had gone wrong. They thought we'd planned it. They thought the affogato was the concept. They thought the beef was free range from the laneway.

Everyone was locked in. Front of house, the bar, Kev, Benny, the girl doing the cold section who I'm pretty sure ran on adrenaline and spite from 9am to close. Nobody complained. Nobody sent a dish back. Nobody even noticed.

Because that's what a service actually is, when you strip it back: it's a hundred and forty people having a good time, and every single one of them is standing between you and the thing going wrong. You just have to be the one holding the shape of it together long enough.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. That's the actual operating model. Put that on the wall somewhere.

**Ice Cold Lad.**

Now. The Melbourne Cup. My horse. I named him Ice Cold Lad, because what else was I going to call him after that week, and because the universe has been taking the piss on me for a fortnight and I decided to meet it halfway.

He came second last.

Second last, Jonno. Out of the whole field. With a name like Ice Cold Lad. The bookies had him at 150-1 and he delivered every penny of that.

I don't know what the universe is doing but it's not subtle about it.

**And now, the bit you're actually waiting for.**

You'd have loved this.

You'd have absolutely loved this, and that's the problem, because you weren't here and you didn't get to see any of it, and instead you get to read about it in a blog post like you're reading about someone else's holiday. That's London for you. That's the whole deal. You moved down there in February and now you've got a soft little office job and a flat with a view of a road and you've never carried thirty kilos of beef shin down a laneway in the rain in your life.

You're soft now, Jonno. Don't argue with me. London made you soft. You text me about lamb. You sent me a photo of a sourdough crumb last week like it meant something. You have opinions about flat whites now. Actual opinions, with a handle on them. You're the sort of bloke who says "oh, that must have been tough" about a story instead of just turning up with a milk crate and a bag of ice and a bad wheel.

You'd have cried, honestly. You would have cried at about 11am, when we opened the walk-in and saw the temperature, and then you'd have said "right, what's the plan" and been completely useless, but you'd have said it, and I would have had to look at you and go, "Jonno, mate. Just carry the crate."

And it wouldn't have been the same without you in it. That's the annoying bit. It genuinely wouldn't have been the same.

**Thursday 12 November.** You said you might come home for a few days in December? If you do, come on a Sunday. Bring a milk crate. Don't bring any of that London softness, we're not running a restaurant for one. We can go to the pub on Smith Street and I'll tell you about the panna cotta and you can tell me about your flat and your office and your sourdough opinions and I'll look at you and I'll say "you've gone soft, Jonno" and you'll say "yeah, I know, mate" and I'll buy you a beer and it'll be fine.

If you don't come home, that's fine too. Just stop asking me for the story and reading it in instalments like a novel. It's one post. It's all in here. You missed the wheel coming off. You missed the servo guy. You missed fourteen bags of ice. You missed table nine and her free range beef.

Come home ya flog, there's a walk-in that needs watching and a draught I'm not paying for.

— Me

*P.S. If you share this with anyone from the restaurant I will 86 your staff meal for a month and you know I have that power.*
